overview: Salt Carbon Fund is NOT an operating company. It is an NZX-listed managed investment scheme (unit trust, part of the Salt Listed Funds scheme) whose sole substantive asset is New Zealand Units (NZUs) — the compliance carbon credits of the NZ Emissions Trading Scheme (NZ ETS). Launched 7 November 2018 at $1.0000/unit as New Zealand's first NZX-listed carbon fund, it is managed by Salt Investment Funds Limited (part of Salt Funds Management, acquired by Alvarium (NZ) Wealth Management Holdings, now SPH Wealth Holdings, on 1 September 2025) and supervised by The New Zealand Guardian Trust Company. The fund's entire investment case is a single-factor bet on the traded price of NZUs; it has no products, customers, competitors in a commercial sense, revenue growth story, or operating margin to analyze.

business_model.summary: The fund raises capital by issuing units on the NZX, uses the proceeds to buy and hold NZUs (and, since the June 2025 mandate widening, potentially Treasury Units and 'Carbon-Related Businesses'), and its Net Tangible Assets (NTA) per unit moves essentially one-for-one with the NZU spot price. There is no operating revenue: NZUs pay no coupon, dividend or yield. The fund's only 'income' is negligible interest on any uninvested cash. Historically the fund did not distribute income to unitholders ('We do not currently intend to make distributions'); the June 2025 PDS update softened this to 'We may make distributions,' but no distribution policy has yet been implemented. Value is realised only by selling units on the NZX or by the manager buying back units (see Treasury Units below), not by any business cash flow.

revenue_streams.name: NZU mark-to-market (unrealised/realised gains on carbon credit holdings)

business_model.customer_type: Retail and institutional NZ investors seeking listed, liquid(ish) exposure to the NZU carbon price without needing an NZ ETS emissions unit account
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% New Zealand — the fund's only real market exposure is the NZ ETS; there is no meaningful international operation (the PDS references possible offshore carbon exposure but the fund has historically held NZUs)

main_competitors: Direct NZU ownership via an EPA-administered Holding Account (skips fund fees and the fund's premium/discount risk)
Forestry/land-based carbon generation vehicles (e.g., forestry-backed and native-forest carbon investment schemes such as MyNativeForest, MyFarm forestry carbon)
Other listed/unlisted managed funds with ETS or carbon exposure (none directly comparable and listed on NZX at present — CO2.NZ remains the only NZX-listed pure-play NZU vehicle)
Global voluntary/compliance carbon ETFs and funds (different underlying commodity, imperfect substitute)
competitive_position.market_position: Sole NZX-listed, pure-play, exchange-traded vehicle for NZU exposure — a structural niche/monopoly on the NZX rather than a competitively contested market position. FUM approximately NZ$65 million as of 31 March 2026 (small/micro-cap fund).

moat_factors.factor: First-mover / only listed NZU vehicle on NZX
moat_factors.description: Convenience for investors who want listed, brokerage-account exposure to NZUs without opening an EPA Holding Account and self-custodying units; this is a structural niche rather than an economic moat, and the 'moat' can be bypassed entirely by direct NZU ownership
Salt/SPH Wealth provide custody (Apex), registry (MUFG) and compliance scaffolding, but this is a service that could in principle be replicated or replaced

weaknesses: No pricing power, no brand premium, no network effects — the product is a pass-through wrapper on a single commodity price
Extremely small, illiquid market (~4,000 units/day, ~NZ$6,000/day traded value) means the NZX quote can drift materially away from published daily NTA
Persistent treasury-unit buying is steadily shrinking the fund (units on issue effectively down from 47.18m to ~20.9m by end-July 2026), raising long-run viability/scale questions
1.0% annual management fee is a certain, compounding drag on a non-yielding, zero-revenue asset

growth_drivers: NZU spot price appreciation is the only real driver of NAV growth — there is no organic/operational growth lever

June 2025 mandate widening to include 'Carbon-Related Businesses' as an authorised investment could, if used, diversify the fund beyond a pure NZU price bet, but no such investments have been disclosed as of the FY2026 annual report

NZU supply scarcity: EPA data shows the stockpile of NZUs in private accounts has fallen materially (down ~9.5 million units year-on-year per mid-2026 reporting) as historic surplus supply is worked through, which is currently supporting spot prices well above the FY2026 year-end low
Continued below-NAV treasury unit buybacks are NAV-per-unit accretive to remaining holders even though they shrink the fund's absolute size

Long-run NZ climate policy requires the ETS (or a successor mechanism) to keep tightening unit caps toward net-zero 2050, which is a structural (if politically contested) tailwind for NZU scarcity value over a multi-decade horizon

business.description: Trading volume is only ~4,000 units/day (~NZ$6,000 notional); the quoted NZX price can be stale, wide, or disconnected from the fund's own published daily NTA for extended periods, creating large execution risk for any investor needing to buy or sell more than a token amount

The fund has repurchased units in every year since FY2023 and never sold any — treasury units rose from 2.81% (FY2023) to 52.65% of units on issue (FY2026), and further buying through mid-2026 has taken outstanding units from 47.18m to ~20.9m. While NAV-accretive to remaining holders, this progressively shrinks the fund toward a scale where it may become uneconomic to run or subject to wind-up/delisting
100% of NAV is effectively one commodity (NZUs); there is no diversification benefit within the fund itself
NZUs generate no yield; historically the fund made no distributions at all, so total return depends entirely on NZU price appreciation and the buy/sell spread an investor achieves on the NZX

financial.risk: Management fee drag on a non-yielding asset
financial.description: A 1.0% p.a. management/administration fee is charged against NAV every year with no offsetting income to fund it (NZUs pay no coupon/dividend), meaning the fund needs the NZU price to rise by more than ~1% annually just to keep pace with a static carbon price, on top of any fee erosion already embedded in historical NAV performance

financial.risk: No leverage disclosed, but no material offsetting financial risk mitigants either
financial.description: The fund does not appear to use debt/leverage; risk is dominated by the underlying commodity, not fund balance-sheet risk

regulatory.risk: NZ ETS policy risk (the dominant risk factor)
regulatory.description: The NZU price is fundamentally a POLICY-SET price, not a free market fundamental. The government controls unit supply caps, the Auction Reserve Price (floor, NZ$71 in 2026, rising to NZ$87 by 2030) and the Cost Containment Reserve (ceiling, ~NZ$201 in 2026 before extra units are released). Historically, government decisions to reject Climate Change Commission advice (December 2022), to set conservative auction volumes, and — most recently — the government's November 2025 decision to remove the legislative link between ETS settings and NZ's Paris Agreement Nationally Determined Contribution, have triggered abrupt double-digit percentage price collapses (NZU spot fell ~20% intraday, from ~NZ$51.50 to ~NZ$41.50, on the November 2025 announcement alone)

All four quarterly NZU government auctions failed to clear in 2023 (zero Crown auction revenue), and secondary-market prices have remained below the auction floor through much of 2025-2026, signalling weak underlying demand relative to the government's price-support settings and creating headline risk that further depresses sentiment

Ongoing debate over whether/when agricultural emissions enter the ETS, and over forestry offset settings (permanent vs. transitional forest categories, carbon farming rules), is a major swing factor for future NZU supply/demand that remains unresolved

June 2025 Master Trust Deed and PDS changes (Treasury Unit powers, removal of certain NZX Listing Rule protections such as the Supervisor's ability to remove the Manager for breach) modestly reduce unitholder protections relative to the prior structure

macro.risk: NZ dollar / no material FX exposure
macro.description: NZUs and the fund are both NZD-denominated so currency risk is minimal for NZ-resident investors, though the PDS references a 'target of full NZD hedging' implying some offshore exposure is contemplated under the widened mandate
NZ ETS is a domestic scheme not directly linked to the EU ETS or other international carbon markets, limiting (but not eliminating) global carbon-price contagion risk

macro.risk: General risk appetite / illiquid micro-cap discount risk
macro.description: In risk-off periods, thinly-traded NZX micro-caps like CO2.NZ can see their quoted price diverge further from NTA due to a lack of market-makers or active liquidity providers

execution.description: Salt Funds Management was acquired by Alvarium (NZ) Wealth Management Holdings (now SPH Wealth Holdings) on 1 September 2025, with a full board refresh (Kate Armstrong and Paul Harrison replaced by Mei Fong, Shane Edmond and Brett Gamble). No change to investment strategy has been disclosed, but new ownership introduces some uncertainty about long-term commitment to running a small, shrinking, fee-light fund

Multiple service-provider changes in FY2025-26 (Administrator changed to Apex Investment Administration (NZ) Limited; Registrar changed to MUFG Pension and Market Services; Apex appointed as custodian) — routine but worth monitoring for operational continuity

macro_factors.industry_outlook: The NZ ETS is a mandatory, government-run cap-and-trade compliance market covering most of New Zealand's gross emissions. Government auction supply is being progressively reduced over time and the Auction Reserve Price floor rises each year (NZ$71 in 2026 → NZ$87 by 2030) by policy design, which should mechanically support higher NZU prices over the medium term IF the government maintains ETS credibility. However, near-term auction failures (all four 2023 auctions and much of 2025 failed to clear) show secondary market prices can trade below the government's own floor when confidence in the scheme's policy trajectory is low.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High — the NZU price has been extremely volatile: from ~$1.00 fund launch level (2018) to a peak of ~NZ$88/tonne (late 2022), a collapse to the ~$33-55 range through 2023-2026, briefly touching as low as $33 in January 2026 before a scarcity-driven rally to the mid-$50s by August 2026. NAV per unit has mirrored this: FY2022 year-end 2.1971 (near the cycle peak) down to FY2026 year-end 1.3786 (-21% for the year), before recovering to an NTA near $1.72 by early August 2026 on the post-March 2026 scarcity rally.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low direct sensitivity — NZUs are a non-yielding physical/administrative commodity, not a discounted cash flow asset, so they are not classically rate-sensitive in the way bonds or growth equities are. Indirect sensitivity exists via general risk appetite and via any effect of rates on forestry/land economics that influence NZU supply from forestry offsets.
key_input_costs: None in the traditional sense — the fund's only 'cost' is the 1.0% p.a. management/administration fee charged against NAV; there is no COGS, no supply chain, no commodity input feeding a production process

recent_developments.event: NZX-quoted market price ~NZ$1.546 (10 Aug 2026, on very thin volume of ~4,000 units) versus the fund's own published daily NTA of approximately NZ$1.719-1.72 (6-7 Aug 2026) — the illiquid market quote is trading at roughly a 10% DISCOUNT to the current published NAV, not a premium, reflecting a lag between the thinly-traded NZX price and the sharp NZU-driven NAV recovery since the 31 March 2026 low

Units on issue reduced to 20,927,948 by 30 July 2026 (from 47,176,460 at 31 March 2026) via continued treasury unit purchases; small on-market buybacks continued through June-July 2026 (e.g., 3 June: 27,781 units at $1.3467; 6 July: 1,364 units at $1.4446; 13 July: 23,519 units at $1.4370), all executed below the then-prevailing NTA

NZU spot price fell as low as ~NZ$33/tonne in mid-January 2026, rallied to ~$48 by late February, and recovered further to ~NZ$54-56/tonne by early August 2026 on 'unusual scarcity' — EPA data show the NZU stockpile in private accounts down ~9.5 million units year-on-year — even though the price remains well below the NZ$71 2026 government Auction Reserve Price floor

FY2026 Annual Report (year ended 31 March 2026) confirms NAV per unit fell from $1.7463 to $1.3786 (-21%) over the fiscal year and that the Carbon Fund bought 9,492,031 of its own units during the year, taking treasury units to 52.65% of units on issue with none ever sold

NZ Government announced removal of the legislative link between NZ ETS unit supply/price settings and the country's Paris Agreement Nationally Determined Contribution — NZU spot price fell ~20% intraday (from ~NZ$51.50-51.70 to as low as ~NZ$41.50) as the market judged the move 'unsupportive of a credible ETS'; this is the single largest identifiable driver of the FY2026 NAV decline

Salt Funds Management (the ultimate parent of the Manager, Salt Investment Funds Limited) was acquired by Alvarium (NZ) Wealth Management Holdings Limited, subsequently renamed SPH Wealth Holdings Limited, effective 1 September 2025; the Manager's board was fully refreshed (Kate Armstrong and Paul Harrison replaced by Mei Fong, Shane Edmond and Brett Gamble)

PDS, SIPO and Master Trust Deed updated: added 'Treasury Units' and 'Carbon-Related Businesses' as authorised investments/objectives; changed distribution policy language from 'We do not currently intend to make distributions' to 'We may make distributions'; added disclosure of daily NTA announcements to NZX; changed Administrator to Apex Investment Administration (NZ) Limited and Registrar to MUFG Pension and Market Services; removed certain NZX Listing Rule-derived unitholder/Supervisor protections following the relevant Listing Rules being repealed

PDS risk indicator for the Carbon Fund reduced from '7' to '6' (effective from the 7 May 2024 PDS update, reported in the FY2025 annual report), reflecting reduced realised volatility versus the 2022-23 collapse period

guidance.as_of: FY2026 Annual Report (year ended 31 March 2026) and NZX daily NTA announcements through 6 August 2026

items.target: No formal management guidance issued — NAV is a mechanical mark-to-market of NZU holdings at the prevailing spot price and management does not forecast or guide NAV
items.notes: As a passive commodity-tracking fund, Salt does not provide forward NAV, earnings, revenue or margin guidance of the kind an operating company would. The only 'guidance' investors receive is the fund's stated investment objective (total return exposure to NZU price movements) and periodic manager commentary in fund updates/factsheets on NZ ETS policy developments.

items.target: May make distributions (changed June 2025 from 'do not currently intend to')
items.notes: No distribution has actually been declared as of the FY2026 annual report; this remains a policy option rather than a commitment

guidance.management_commentary: The FY2026 Annual Report (a Scheme-level compliance document, not a narrative report) contains no forward-looking commentary on NZU price expectations, ETS policy views, or fund strategy beyond the factual disclosures on unit numbers, treasury buybacks, related-party holdings, and governance/service-provider changes noted above. Detailed manager commentary, if any, would appear in the quarterly Fund Updates and factsheets on carbonfund.co.nz, which were not obtained for this analysis.

bull_case: NAV has already recovered sharply from the FY2026 (31 March 2026) low of $1.3786 to a published NTA near $1.72 by early August 2026 as NZU spot prices rallied on tightening private-account supply — the current NZX market quote (~$1.546) appears to lag this recovery, so a buyer today may be acquiring exposure at roughly a 10% discount to the fund's own stated NAV
Persistent below-NAV treasury unit buybacks (over half of all units now held in treasury, with continued purchases through July 2026) are mechanically NAV-per-unit accretive to remaining holders

Structural long-run ETS design (a falling unit cap and a rising Auction Reserve Price floor through 2030) provides a policy-engineered scarcity tailwind for NZU prices if the government maintains scheme credibility
The fund is the only NZX-listed, easily tradeable vehicle for NZU exposure, giving investors listed/brokerage-account access to an asset class otherwise requiring a dedicated EPA Holding Account

NZU prices are currently well below their 2022 peak (~$88) and below the government's own 2026 auction floor (~$71), which some investors may view as offering asymmetric upside if ETS settings are perceived as credible again
bear_case: NZU price — and therefore fund NAV — is fundamentally a government policy variable, not a market fundamental; the November 2025 NDC-delinking announcement alone erased ~20% of the NZU price in a single session, illustrating how a single policy decision can destroy a large fraction of unitholder value overnight with no diversification to cushion it

Extreme illiquidity (~4,000 units/day, ~NZ$6,000 notional traded) means the quoted NZX price can and does diverge materially from published daily NTA in either direction, creating real execution risk and making the fund unsuitable for any meaningful position size without accepting a wide effective spread

The fund pays no income and has essentially never distributed cash; total return depends entirely on achieving a favourable buy/sell price on a thinly-traded exchange, with no yield to cushion drawdowns
The 1.0% p.a. management fee is a certain, compounding drag against a zero-yield asset, permanently eroding NAV relative to the raw NZU price every year regardless of market conditions

The fund is shrinking rapidly via treasury buybacks (units on issue down from 47.2 million to ~20.9 million between 31 March 2026 and 30 July 2026, more than a 55% reduction) — if this continues, the fund risks becoming sub-scale, uneconomic to administer, or a candidate for wind-up/delisting, which is a structural overhang distinct from the NZU price itself

Repeated NZ government auction failures (all four 2023 auctions, and much of 2025-2026) show that policy-set floor prices are not always supported by secondary market demand, undermining the case that ETS design mechanically puts a floor under NZU (and hence NAV) prices
